newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria in limbo awaits word from new leader.
newsitem.headline: Austria in limbo awaits word from new leader.

text.p: Austrian politics were in a state of limbo on Sunday as outgoing chancellor Franz Vranitzky bid farewell after a decade in office and the nation awaited the first words from his elusive successor, Viktor Klima.

Klima, not previously known for timidity before the media, vanished from public view after Vranitzky unexpectedly announced his resignation on Saturday after almost 11 years and named him as his chosen successor.

The Social Democrats announced that the popular 49-year-old finance minister would break his silence at a news conference with Vranitzky outside Vienna on Monday. But less than an hour later, the meeting was cancelled.
Klima's immediate tasks are to outline his policies to his Social Democratic Party and choose his ministerial line-up.
The appointment of a new finance minister will be seen as crucial, but has already stirred up the concerns of the conservative People's Party, the junior coalition partner.

People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel, clearly slighted by not being informed of Vranitzky's decision to resign, insists on a say in the choice but senior Social Democrats say this is out of the question.

Vranitzky, Europe's second longest-serving leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, looked visibly relieved to be handing over the reins to his bright second-in-command after years of political wrangling with Schuessel's party.

Vranitzky's leadership was widely attacked as stale and lacking in innovation and political commentators heralded Klima's appointment as a chance to bring a much-needed breath of fresh air to the nation's top post.
At a valedictory news conference, Vranitzky, 59, took stock of his achievements and failures.

"I think my greatest success was to take Austria into the European Union," he said, adding that one of his greatest challenges was to cope with the changing face of Europe in the post-Cold War period.
He will also go down in history for publicly acknowledging on a visit to Israel in 1993 that Austria shared responsibility for atrocities committed by Hitler's Nazi regime.
On the debit side, Vranitzky said his party might have failed to react quickly enough to the fast-growing popularity of Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party.
"Perhaps the Social Democrats were a bit too late and did not do enough to unmask his strategy of demonising human beings or organisations," he said.
The Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low in European elections last October, dipping below 30 percent, while support for the far right has soared to nearly 28 percent.
The leadership change followed a bitter row with the conservatives over the sale of Creditanstalt, Austria's second biggest bank, which had threatened to destroy the coalition.
Klima, who will be Austria's eighth chancellor since 1945, emerged last week as one of the chief victors in the tussle, unscathed by the mudslinging of the party leaders.
